topic: Prescription quality and WHO prescribing indicators

audits.title: Improving rational medicine prescribing at a public district hospital in southwestern Uganda, January–November 2021: a quality improvement initiative
audits.standard: Uganda Clinical Guidelines (UCG) prescribing concordance and rational medicine use indicators
audits.setting: Public district hospital in southwestern Uganda, outpatients

cycle1.result: Guideline-concordant prescribing 43.7%; antibiotic prescribing 83.4%; mean 3.35 medicines per encounter; generic-only prescriptions 78.6%.

audits.intervention: Prescriber education, soft-copy UCG and essential medicines lists, prescribing restricted to recognised clinicians with signature verification, and periodic prescription audit and feedback.

cycle2.result: Guideline-concordant prescribing 76.2% (aPR=1.82); antibiotic prescribing 65.3%; 2.66 medicines per encounter; generic-only 94.1%.

audits.other_findings: Antibiotic use remained high despite improvement.
audits.citation: Migisha R, Namasambi S, Kwesiga B, Bulage L, Ario AR. Improving rational medicine prescribing at a public district hospital in southwestern Uganda, January–November 2021: a quality improvement initiative. . 2026. doi:10.64898/2026.09.02.26361584.

audits.title: Prescription Audit in Outpatient Pharmacy of a Tertiary Care Referral Hospital in Haryana Using Who/ Inrud Core Prescribing Indicators: A Step Towards Refining Drug Use and Patient Care
audits.setting: Outpatient pharmacy, tertiary care referral hospital, Haryana

cycle1.result: Mean 3.03 drugs per prescription; 75% generic names; antibiotic in 20.59%; injectables in 1.15%; 55.4% from the National List of Essential Medicines; IRDP 3.86.

audits.other_findings: High polypharmacy, brand name and non-essential drug prescribing; antibiotic and injection use in line with WHO standards.
audits.citation: Verma N, Vinayagam S, Mittal N, Mittal R, Bansal N. Prescription Audit in Outpatient Pharmacy of a Tertiary Care Referral Hospital in Haryana Using Who/ Inrud Core Prescribing Indicators: A Step Towards Refining Drug Use and Patient Care. . 2025. doi:10.20944/preprints202501.1150.v1.

audits.title: To analyze the Impact of Serial Prescription Audits with Active Feedback on Quality of Prescription Behaviour.
audits.standard: WHO Guide to Good Prescribing, WHO drug core indicators and the updated WHO Essential Medicines list
audits.setting: Outpatient departments of Jhalawar Medical College and Hospital and Chintpurni Medical College and Hospital

cycle1.result: Baseline prescription audit on the last date of the first month of each cycle (n=250 prescriptions per month); figures not reported in the abstract.

audits.intervention: Monthly continuous evaluation with active feedback on conformity to WHO prescribing guidance.

cycle2.result: Significant improvement in completeness and rationality of prescription formats at the end of the 2nd and 3rd months of each cycle; WHO drug core indicators improved with every re-audit in each cycle (p value truncated in abstract).

audits.other_findings: Four 3-month cycles over two years, each followed by three months without audit; stopping the audits began to reverse the improvement in prescribing behaviour.
audits.citation: Jyoti N, Kaur S. To analyze the Impact of Serial Prescription Audits with Active Feedback on Quality of Prescription Behaviour. J Clin Diagn Res. 2013;7(4):680-683. doi:10.7860/jcdr/2013/5441.2880. PMID: 23730645.

audits.title: Prescription Audit in Outpatient Pharmacy of a Tertiary Care Referral Hospital in Haryana Using World Health Organization/International Network of Rational Use of Drugs (WHO/INRUD) Core Prescribing Indicators: A Step Towards Refining Drug Use and Patient Care.
audits.setting: Outpatient pharmacy, Pt. B.D. Sharma PGIMS, Rohtak; tertiary care referral hospital

cycle1.result: Mean 3.03 drugs per prescription; 75% generic names; antibiotics in 20.59%; injectables in 1.15%; 55.4% of drugs on the NLEM 2022.

audits.other_findings: Index of rational drug prescribing 3.86; polypharmacy, brand-name and non-essential drug prescribing were high, while antibiotic and injection use met WHO standards.
audits.citation: Verma N, Vinayagam S, Mittal N, Mittal R, Bansal N. audits.title: Outpatient prescribing trends, rational use of medicine and impact of prescription audit with feedback at a tertiary care centre in India.
audits.standard: WHO core prescribing indicators: drugs per prescription ≤2; antibiotics ≤30%; injections ≤10%; generic and NLEM prescribing 100%
audits.setting: Outpatient departments, AIIMS Bhopal tertiary care centre

cycle1.result: Mean 2.53 ± 1.23 drugs per prescription; antibiotics 19.82%; injections 1.98%; generic prescribing 15.96%; NLEM prescribing 37.37%.

cycle2.result: Improvement in generic prescribing and prescribing from NLEM; other trends similar.

audits.other_findings: Antibiotic and injection use were within WHO optimal values.
audits.citation: Atal S, Jhaj R, Mathur A, Rai N, Misra S, Sadasivam B. Outpatient prescribing trends, rational use of medicine and impact of prescription audit with feedback at a tertiary care centre in India. Int J Health Plann Manage. 2021;36(3):738-753. doi:10.1002/hpm.3116. PMID: 33491843.
